## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Āsavakkhaya Sutta* ("The Ending of Defilements", Iti 102) is a discourse found in the four-fold division (Catukkanipāta) of the *Itivuttaka* [SuttaCentral]. The text presents a concise exposition on the attainment of liberation, declaring that the destruction of the defilements (*āsavakkhaya*) belongs to one who knows and sees rather than to one who does not [SuttaCentral]. This liberating destruction of suffering is achieved specifically through knowing and seeing the four noble truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the practice leading to its cessation [SuttaCentral]. None of the secondary passages in the reference dossier examine Iti 102 directly; references in the surveyed literature either discuss the doctrinal category of *āsavakkhaya* (the destruction of the taints as the final *abhiññā* or arahantship) or analyze other discourses sharing the same formula [SuttaCentral].

SuttaCentral identifies passage-level parallels in the *Sacca Saṁyutta* (SN 56.25, *Āsavakkhayasutta*), the *Sabbāsava Sutta* (MN 2), the *Upanisasutta* (SN 12.23), the *Vāsijaṭasutta* (SN 22.101), the *Sekkhasutta* (AN 3.85), *Itivuttaka* 62 (*Indriya Sutta*), and a Chinese counterpart at T 765.132 [SuttaCentral]. The discourse is additionally cited in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 2.2, *Aññāṇakathā*, and Kv 2.3, *Kaṅkhākathā*) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus matches strongly corroborate these textual links, recording extensive Pali-internal reuse between Iti 102 and SN 56.25 (segment §1.1–2.4 ↔ §25.0.3–25.1.4) as well as the *Kathāvatthu* discussions in Kv 2.3 (§2.1–2.3_1 ↔ §17.4–17.8), Kv 2.2 (§2.1–2.4 ↔ §28.4–28.11), and Kv 2.4 (*Paravitāraṇakathā*) [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages with the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 14), MN 2, and the commentary *Itivuttaka-aṭṭhakathā*, along with recurrent framing prose shared across neighboring discourses of the *Itivuttaka* (such as Iti 101, Iti 103, and Iti 108–112) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records sixteen translations across fourteen languages, including an English translation by Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral].

*No discussion of this text was found in the reference-literature corpus; the overview relies on SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus data.*
